Flash memory cells are very different from the memory we use to create main system memory; specifically, flash cells, while cheaper, are considerably slower than DDR4 RAM chips, and suffer from degradation over many write cycles.

Using SSD space as system memory is not an entirely new concept; Using the systems main storage device in place of memory is done by most operating systems via a Swap file. Many linux machines have a separate partition just for this swap file. If you measure performance, swapping to an SSD is certainly faster than swapping to a hard drive, but is still several orders of magnitude slower than traditional DDR3/DDR4 memory operations. This is, in part, due to the sata interface, but this problem will still manifest itself on m.2 nvme ssds. The fact of the matter is, flash cells are not suitable to replace system memory. They are too slow, and, with the frequency memory gets written to, a system that forgoes RAM entirely for an SSD will find itself wearing out SSDs pretty quickly.

Think about it this way. You are playing a videogame. Lets say Minecraft. Every now and then, you save the game, which will go through and save numeric coordinates stating your position, the position and identity of every mob in the map, and the position, identity, and other properties of every block on the map. This takes roughly a quarter second, if saving to an SSD.

Still with me?

Minecraft, like any other game, processes time by going through a giant loop. Each iteration of the loop (called a tick), takes 1/20th of a second. During each tick, the game checks the player's current velocity, checks the players position, adds the velocity to the current position, calculated field of view, updates changes to blocks .etc. Effectively, it loads the game from RAM, updates it a tiny bit, and saves it back to RAM, all in that single tick. If it can't complete all this in the 1/20th of a second timewindow, we get lag. Remember that saving the game to an SSD (and just saving it, not performing other calculations, or loading it), takes about 1/4th of a second. This just wouldn't work, if the only place available to store current gamestate information was the SSD.

TL;DR. SSDs are much slower than system memory, and also can't stand up to repeated write operations like what's demanded of RAM.

That's part of it. Main storage gets overwritten at a much slower rate; An entire memory module can have every bit overwritten on it several million times a second, whereas writing over every bit of 16 gigs of ssd space might take 10 minutes or so. Additionally, ssds manage this by having what we call wear leveling- when I write a file to an ssd, it goes to one set of flash cells, but when I edit the file, it will get rewritten to another, so that all the flash cells wear out evenly. They also have additional space that's hidden from the user to aid in this. Such wear leveling would cause problems for applications, which rely on what we call "Pointers" quite a bit for their code to work right. Pointers effectively say "Hey, look at something at this memory address, specifically." pointers wouldn't exactly work on a flash cell for that reason (unless the operating system properly managed the cells with a swap file); the address of the individual variable referenced by the pointer would likely change every single time the variable's value was reassigned.
